What a marketing report should actually tell you

If your monthly report is full of impressions and click-through rates, it is answering the wrong questions. Here are the five it should answer instead.

Why most reports don’t help

Owners of service businesses are busy. A twelve-page report full of impressions, reach and click-through rates is easy to file and hard to act on. The numbers aren’t wrong; they just answer questions the owner isn’t asking.

A useful report is short, starts with money, and ends with a decision.

That doesn’t mean the detail is useless. It means it belongs to a different audience. The person running the ads needs platform metrics every day; the owner needs to know, once a month, whether marketing is producing profitable work and what will change next. Mixing the two in one document serves neither of them well.

The five questions

  1. What did marketing produce in booked revenue? Not leads, not calls: jobs and their value.
  2. Which sources produced it? So budget can follow results.
  3. What did it cost to win? Spend divided by booked jobs, by source.
  4. Where did we lose opportunities? Missed calls, unconverted estimates, slow follow-up.
  5. What are we changing next month? One to three decisions, with an owner.

“If a report doesn’t change a decision, it’s a status update.”

A one-page layout that works

Example structure for a one-page monthly report
SectionWhat goes in it
HeadlineBooked revenue from marketing, compared to last month and last year
By sourceJobs, revenue and cost per job for each channel
LeaksMissed calls, open estimates, response time
DecisionsWhat changes next month and who owns it
AppendixPlatform metrics for the people managing campaigns

What about clicks and impressions?

They still matter, to the people running campaigns. Click-through rate helps a media buyer improve an ad. It doesn’t help an owner decide whether to hire another technician. Keep those metrics, but move them to an appendix.

In practice · Roofing

Storm-season reports that lead with signed contracts by source and inspection-to-contract rate, with ad metrics on the last page.

Getting the data you need

Most of the numbers in a good report live in two places: the CRM, which knows where a lead came from, and the field-service or accounting software, which knows what the job was worth. Joining them, even manually, is the single most valuable reporting task.

Signs your report needs work

  • It takes more than five minutes to find out how many jobs marketing produced.
  • The same numbers appear every month with no comment on what changed.
  • Nobody can say what decision was made because of last month’s report.
  • Revenue appears nowhere, or only as a total with no breakdown by source.

None of these mean the team behind the report is doing a bad job. They usually mean the report was designed around what was easy to export, not around what the business needs to know. Redesigning it around the five questions is a one-off piece of work that pays back every month.

It also changes the conversation with whoever runs your marketing. When the report starts with booked revenue, discussions move from “why did clicks drop?” to “how do we get more of the jobs that pay best?”, which is where an owner’s attention belongs.

This month’s homework

  1. Ask your team or agency to answer the five questions on one page.
  2. If they can’t, find out which data is missing and fix that first.
  3. End your next review by writing down one decision.

Key takeaways

  • A report should lead to a decision, not just describe activity.
  • Start with booked revenue, then work backwards to activity.
  • Keep platform metrics in an appendix for the people who manage them.
  • Every report should end with what changes next month.
